activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
story:
The sign-up sheet said the class debate team tryout would end at 3:15, and it was already 2:50. Elliot stood in the hallway outside Ms. Guo's room, gripping his notes, while Marylou and Niko argued in front of him about who should go first.

"You go," Niko said. "You're the one who said the cafeteria pizza is the worst food in the state."

"That's not something you can test," Elliot said suddenly. "You can't prove it true or false. It's just what I believe, what I feel about pizza." The words came out before he thought about them, and they reminded him of last winter, sitting at the kitchen table while his older brother insisted their uncle's chili was objectively disgusting. His father had leaned over the pot and said, "Give me one test for that, kid." His brother couldn't, and had finally laughed and admitted maybe it was just his tongue against the chili. That night, the whole argument had collapsed into nothing, and everyone had gotten seconds.

Elliot's tryout topic was on the sheet in his hand: "Our school's new rule restricting backpacks in hallways is unfair." He had ten minutes to prepare, and now his notes looked strange to him. "Unfair" was a judgment, the kind of thing evidence couldn't prove. But parts of the rule could be checked. Whether students actually got hurt by backpacks in the hall was something you could count. Whether other schools had the same rule was something you could look up.

When Ms. Guo called him in, he spread his notes on the desk. "I want to argue the backpack rule," he said, "but I have to be honest about what's a claim and what's an opinion. The claim is that hallway accidents dropped after the rule. That can be checked against the accident log in the office, and shown true or false. The unfair part is my opinion. Evidence can't prove it, but it can still be my judgment."

Ms. Guo raised an eyebrow. "You'd give up the easy part, the part that gets applause?"

"It felt naive to think nobody would notice the difference," Elliot said. "Someone on the other team would."

She slid a visitor badge across the desk. "The office closes at 3:15, same as tryouts. If you want that accident log, you have about fifteen minutes." Elliot grabbed the badge and ran, sneakers squeaking on the tile, and behind him he heard Marylou shouting, "Check if they restrict lunch passes too!"

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
The trouble had started on Tuesday, when Mr. Ndlovu pulled Callan and Michael aside after the drama club meeting and said they would perform a two-person scene at the spring showcase, no script, no plan. Michael had wanted a part with lines he could memorize. Instead he got "improv," a word that sounded like something you did right before falling off a cliff.

By Saturday he was in the living room with Callan and Aanya, a note from Mr. Ndlovu folded on the coffee table. Michael read it out loud for the third time. "Dear Michael. In our game, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem. Your job is to catch every offer and say yes, and. P.S. Your last practice was painful to watch. Sincerely, Mr. Ndlovu." Aanya laughed so hard she slid off the arm of the couch.

"Let's just try it," Callan said, standing up. He pointed one finger at the carpet, reeled an invisible line in with careful, patient hands.

"Hi," Michael said. "What are you doing?"

Callan lowered the invisible rod. "Dude. Seriously?"

Michael replayed the moment later, while Aanya got juice from the kitchen. Two weeks ago, before the showcase was announced, Callan had done the exact same mime in the gym and Michael had ignored it then too, and Callan had stood there fishing at nothing until the game collapsed. The problem wasn't nerves, Michael realized. It was that his eyes treated the rod as random wiggling instead of information. Callan was handing him a place and a problem and Michael kept dropping them, and every dropped offer made the scene worse in a cumulative way, piling up until there was nothing left to act with. He could not see the offers, exactly, the way you can't see wind, but he could see what they did.

Aanya came back with three cups and set them down. "Okay, one rule," she said. "Michael, before you speak, name the offer out loud. Place, name, or problem. Say it, then respond."

Callan picked up the invisible rod again, cast it across the rug toward the bookshelf.

"Offer," Michael said. "We're fishing, and this is a lake. Yes, and I'll bait your hook with this sandwich, because the fish here have expensive taste." He held out an imaginary sandwich, mayonnaise side up.

Callan grinned and reeled faster. "Careful. The last person who fed the fish opened a restaurant, and now the fish expect to see a menu and a revenue report before they bite."

Aanya clapped once. "See? You didn't cite the rule, you used it."

"Shh," Michael said, keeping his eyes on the line. "The big one's coming. Hand me the sandwich."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
story:
Beatrice had come to the library for one reason: to prove her uncle wrong. At Sunday dinner he had lifted his wrist, rattled the copper bracelet on it, and announced that it had cured his back pain, and that the company had letters from a hundred satisfied customers. Her cousin Finley had nodded along, but Beatrice had gone home with a strange itch in her mind, the kind that meant a question was not finished with her yet.

She found a table near the window where the afternoon light fell across the wood in long pale stripes. Alizee was already there, spreading out books for their science project, and Beatrice flopped into the chair across from her. "I need to ask you something," Beatrice said. "My uncle says his bracelet fixed his back. How would we know if it actually did?"

Alizee tilted her head. "Did he do anything else that week?" Beatrice thought back. He had started swimming at the community pool, and she remembered her aunt saying he'd finally agreed to see a physiotherapist about his knees, something about worn cartilage and exercises. She wrote both of those on a scrap of paper and stared at them. "So maybe the swimming helped," she said slowly. "Or the exercises. Or it would have gotten better anyway."

"That's a story about one person," Alizee said. "My mom calls that an anecdote." She tapped the library's science database on her laptop and pulled up a proper study, one where hundreds of people wore real bracelets or identical fake ones, and neither group knew which was which. Beatrice read the results twice. The two groups had improved about the same, which meant the copper itself could not take the credit.

The itch in her mind quieted. An anecdote, she decided, was like one footprint in the snow: it told you somebody had passed by, but not which path they had taken or why. A study with many people and tested evidence was more like a whole trail, stamped down from every direction until the pattern showed. It wasn't that her uncle was lying; he genuinely felt better. He had just skipped over the part where other explanations get ruled out.

The next weekend she drafted a note, planning to petition the family for a new Sunday dinner rule: every amazing claim had to survive three questions before anyone was allowed to buy anything. Finley thought it was hilarious and signed first. Her uncle read the note, snorted, and slid the bracelet off his wrist. "Fine," he said, setting it on the table with a small copper clink. "But I'm keeping the swimming."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
George had exactly forty minutes to figure out what he was doing wrong before the toasts started at Quincy's sister's wedding.

The reception was in a rented hall behind a Malaysian restaurant, and George was one of only three guests from his school. Quincy had invited him last minute, which meant George hadn't gone to the family dinner where the others had learned whatever they'd learned. He noticed it almost right away: when the flower lady came around, Quincy's grandmother took the little sachet with her right hand. When Uncle somebody passed the tea, he poured and received with his right hand too. George had been handing things back and forth with his left all afternoon, and nobody had said a word, but he caught the grandmother's eyes flick down at his left hand once, twice, and then away.

He remembered a family dinner at Blaine's house in the spring. Blaine's cousin, who was visiting from Kuala Lumpur, had reached for the rice dish with her left hand, and Blaine's mother had touched her wrist and switched the spoon into her right. Nobody explained anything. Blaine had just leaned over and whispered, "In Indonesia and Malaysia, everybody eats and gives and takes with the right hand, out of respect." George had filed it away and forgotten it until now, standing with a gift bag in his left hand and the grandmother heading straight for him.

The problem was the gift. Quincy's family had a table near the front where people were handing over envelopes and boxes before the toasts, and the line was already forming. George had twenty minutes, maybe less. He tested his idea quietly first. When the waiter offered him a satay skewer, George took it with his right hand and said thank you, and the grandmother, watching from her chair, gave him a small nod that looked almost like approval. So it wasn't about being a foreign guest. It was about the hand.

He got in line, shifted the bag into his right hand, and waited. His left palm was sweating around the card he was supposed to pin to the board, which he also moved to his right. When his turn came, he held out the gift with his right hand, and Quincy's sister took it the same way and smiled at him, a real one, not the polite smile she'd given the man before him who had tossed his envelope down with his left.

George walked back to his seat feeling like he'd solved something. Quincy slid over to make room.

"You figured it out," Quincy said.

"Blaine's cousin," George said, and picked up his fork with his right hand, just to keep the streak going.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
Jayden sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with his tablet balanced on a couch cushion, sorting through the basketball stats his league had posted online. Nolan sprawled on the couch above him, tossing a sock ball at the ceiling fan and catching it. Outside, rain ticked against the window, and the lamp made a small symmetrical pattern of light on the floor, half on the rug and half on the wood.

"Look at this," Jayden said, turning the tablet around. "Talya's teammate Priya is listed at the top of the shooting chart. It says one hundred percent."

Nolan leaned over and squinted. "Priya? She barely plays. How is she beating everyone?"

That was the question Jayden wanted to answer too. He scrolled down the column and found the numbers behind the big one. Priya had attempted one shot all season. She had made one shot. He tapped the screen. "She took one shot. One. She made it, so her percentage is perfect."

Nolan flopped back. "That's a weird paradox. She's the best shooter and the worst shooter at the same time."

Jayden remembered the summer before, when his uncle had let him keep score for a pickup game at the park. A man in a red jersey had made his first three and bragged the whole rest of the afternoon, then missed eleven in a row and gone quiet. At the time Jayden had assumed the man was just having a bad stretch after a great start. Now he wondered if the start had ever been as great as it looked.

"Let's test it," Jayden said. He pulled a sock ball from the laundry basket by the couch and set up the waste basket across the room. "I'll shoot ten times. You count." His first shot dropped clean through the rim of the basket. "There. One for one. I'm at one hundred percent, better than Priya."

Nolan grinned and kept counting. The second sock bounced off the arm of the chair. The third sailed wide. By the tenth attempt, Jayden had made four. He did the division in his head and wrote it on the tablet with his finger. "Forty percent. Same guy, same shot, different number."

"So Priya's percentage only looks amazing because she hardly ever shoots," Nolan said, picking up the socks and restuffing them into the basket. "If she took fifty shots, it would probably come out like everybody else's."

Jayden nodded and pulled up the message thread where the whole team argued about the rankings. Talya had been defending Priya's spot at the top all week, mostly because Priya kept bragging in the group chat. He typed a short message, attached a screenshot of the attempts column, and set the tablet face down on the cushion.

The reply came fast, a single line from Talya: "Okay, fine. Priya, take more than one shot at Saturday's game, and then we'll talk."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
story:
Sarah stood on Ivana's porch at ten to six, holding a small box of dates and wondering, for the tenth time, whether she should have brought flowers instead. The invitation had said dinner at six, and Ivana's mother was strict about punctuality, so Sarah rang the bell with two minutes to spare.

Inside the hallway, shoes stood in a tidy row along the wall. Sarah had been to Ivana's house before and knew the rule, so she unlaced her sneakers and set them beside the others. "You brought a gift," Ivana said, spotting the box. "Good. My mom will like that you didn't come empty-handed. Lyna brought something too, tea from home."

Lyna was already sitting at the kitchen table. She had arrived from New Zealand two weeks ago, and Sarah had watched her welcome assembly from the third row of the gym, where the whole school fell quiet when Lyna and Mr. Hu leaned toward each other and pressed their noses and foreheads together. The entire gym had whispered about it afterward, and Sarah had never found out what it meant. Now was her chance, but she wanted to be careful. If she asked in a clumsy way, she might sound like she was laughing at it, and she had done that once before, in fourth grade, with a classmate's lunch, and she still regretted it.

"Can you tell me about the assembly?" Sarah asked, sliding into a chair. "When you and Mr. Hu did that thing with your foreheads. I've been trying to figure it out."

"It's called a hongi," Lyna said. She set down her fork. "It means sharing the breath of life."

Sarah tested the idea in her head, the way she tested a guess in science class. If the greeting was about sharing breath, then it wasn't just a hello, it was more like saying your life and mine are connected now. That would explain why the gym had gone so quiet, why it felt like a ceremony and not a wave or a handshake. "So when Mr. Hu did it with you," she said slowly, "he wasn't just welcoming you to the school. He was saying you belong here."

Lyna smiled. "That's exactly it."

Ivana's mother called everyone to wash hands, and then the food came out in a gradual procession, dish after dish, rice last. Sarah watched how Lyna waited until the older people had served themselves before she took anything, and copied her, holding back her fork even when the dumplings steamed right under her nose.

Later, as Ivana's mother recounted the story of how she had once flooded the kitchen making dumplings, Sarah caught herself leaning forward, forehead first, almost bumping Lyna's shoulder in a pretend hongi, and both of them burst out laughing before anyone could ask why.

"You two are strange," said Ivana, and passed the last dumpling to Lyna.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Telling a trusted adult is not tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble.
story:
The birthday party was in full swing behind Eunice's house, twelve kids crowded around a table of pizza and a cake shaped like a soccer ball, when Easton heard the laughter change pitch. It was the sharp kind of laughter, the kind that condenses into something heavier than fun. Makai stood by the fence holding his plate, and two boys from another school were doing his voice, dragging their words out the way he did when he was excited.

Easton froze, holding his cup. Last month, at the pool, he had watched a kid get dunked repeatedly and said nothing. He had told himself it wasn't his business, but the look on that kid's face had stayed with him, the way steam stays on a mirror. He did not want to see that look on Makai.

He tried the obvious thing first. "Hey, knock it off," he said, stepping between them, but his voice came out too loud and too fast. The two boys grinned wider. "Ooh, bodyguard," one said, and now three kids were laughing at two people instead of one. His plan had made it worse. He could see the pattern: confronting them head-on just gave them a bigger audience.

So he changed his mind about the whole approach. Instead of standing there arguing, he turned and steered Makai toward the pizza table. "You have to try the cake before it's gone," he said, loud enough that everyone heard something normal. The laughter had nothing to land on. It faded, scattered like the crowd when someone turns off the music.

Later, by the recycling bin, he told Eunice what he had seen before, at lunch last week too, the same two boys mimicking Makai. "It keeps happening," Eunice said. "It's not a one-time thing."

"I want to tell Ms. Nwosu," Easton said. Makai's shoulders went stiff. "Then everyone calls me a snitch."

Easton thought about his little sister's vaccine card stuck to the fridge, how a shot was a small sting that stopped something bigger. "It's not tattling," he said slowly, testing the idea as he said it. "Telling a trusted adult is not tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble." He had expected the sentence to sound like something off a poster, but Makai actually looked at him.

"That's the difference?" Makai asked.

"That's the whole difference," Easton said. "Getting them in trouble isn't the point. Making it stop is."

Ms. Nwosu lived two doors down and was already walking over with a bag of ice for the drinks. Easton waved her over, and Makai, after a breath, came with him. Whether it would have been braver to say something at the pool last month, Easton still wasn't sure. He watched Makai start talking, hands moving, voice steady.

"I'll check on it Monday," Ms. Nwosu said, and put the bag of ice in Easton's arms. "Now, who's helping me with the punch?"

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6.
story:
Stella crouched at the top of the gym ramp with a stopwatch in one hand and a marble in the other. Corbin stood at the bottom beside a long tape measure, holding a chalk line where the ball had stopped last time. "Again," he called, so she let the marble go and clicked the timer, then clicked again when it crossed his sneakers. "Six meters, 3.2 seconds," she said, writing it down.

They needed the project for Ms. Takahashi's class: draw a distance-time graph of a rolling ball, then read the speed straight off the line. Stella had already plotted two runs, and the dots made a nearly straight slope, which meant the marble barely slowed on the ramp. But her graph gave the speed in meters per second, and that was where the trouble started.

"Marlon says his paper ball rolled faster than a person walks," Corbin said, peeling the marble off the floor. "He said nobody walks two meters per second." Stella frowned at her notebook. Her marble managed 1.9 meters per second, which sounded slower than every kid in the hallway, and Marlon had spent all of lunch looking smug about it. She wanted a real answer, not a feeling.

The bell rang before she could finish thinking, so she carried the problem to the library and dug through the science shelf until she found a chart of speed conversions. There it was, plain as a lunch menu. To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6. She tested it on her own number right there, pencil scratching in the margin: 1.9 times 3.6 came to 6.84 kilometers per hour.

"Six point eight four kilometers per hour," she announced the next morning, catching Corbin at his locker before he could even shut it. "To change meters per second into kilometers per hour, you multiply by 3.6. It's on the chart in the library." Elyana leaned in from the next locker, chewing the end of her ponytail. "People walk about five kilometers per hour," she said slowly. "So the marble beats a walker." Corbin pumped his fist, and Stella grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

In class, Ms. Takahashi asked who had finished both the graph and the speed calculation, and Stella raised her hand so fast her chair scraped. She pinned her graph to the board, ran her finger up the slope, and said the marble traveled at nearly seven kilometers per hour. Marlon slumped, then laughed, and asked if he could time his paper ball after school. Stella slid the stopwatch across the table toward him. "First we calibrate it," she said, "against the clock on the wall, so nobody's numbers look sinister when they lose."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: The CSS rule h1 { text-align: center; } centres the text of every top-level heading on the page.
story:
Lucy had one hour before the library closed, and her homepage still looked wrong. The heading, "Lucy's Voluntary Trail Crew Journal," sat stubbornly against the left edge of the screen while everything else on the page drifted toward the middle. She had drafted the page twice already at the table by the window, where the late afternoon light made the laptop screen hard to read, so she had moved to the corner by the biography shelves.

Tate slid into the chair across from her and peered at the screen. "It still looks like it's hiding in the corner."

"It's not hiding, it's just stuck." Lucy highlighted the line again, though highlighting had never fixed anything in her life. She had written the style rule exactly the way the handout from Mr. Diallo's coding club showed, or at least she thought she had. Somewhere between the paper handout and her own file, something had changed.

Remi leaned over from the next table, where a stack of returned books waited to be reshelved. "Read me what you typed. Sometimes hearing it helps." Remi was the one who had caught the missing bracket in Lucy's first attempt, back when the whole page had rendered as plain text.

Lucy read it out slowly: "h1, space, then text-align: centre, with r-e at the end." She stopped. Remi's eyebrows went up. Lucy scrolled up to the club handout, which was creased from living in her backpack, and flattened it against the table. There it was, plain as anything: center, spelled the American way. The computer wanted that exact spelling, and it had been quietly refusing her rule the whole time, without leaving a single error message to tell her so.

"You can't see it refusing," Lucy said, mostly to herself. "It just ignores you." That was the strange part, she thought, that a page could look almost right while a hidden spelling rule sat underneath, undoing her work. She deleted the last two letters, typed the e-r, and saved.

The heading glided to the middle of the page as if it had always wanted to be there. Tate actually clapped once, then lowered her hand when a woman at the circulation desk glanced over. Lucy added a second heading lower down, a smaller one about Saturday's trail work, and watched that one slide into place too, since the rule reached every top-level heading on the page, not just the first.

Mr. Diallo came by on his way out with his coat already on. "Staying till close?"

"Till they kick me out," Lucy said, and reached for the handout to draft the next page.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Musical loudness is marked with Italian words: piano means soft and forte means loud.
story:
Cole had played "Ode to Joy" perfectly eleven times in a row, and it sounded completely wrong. Hunter's basement had an old upright piano against the wall, and Hunter's dad had said they could use it until five, so Cole had time, but time wasn't the problem. The problem was that his recital piece had strange little letters scattered through it, and he had been ignoring them.

"You're playing it like a robot," said Hunter, sprawled on the couch with a video game he wasn't really watching. "It's the same the whole way through. Like a doorbell."

Cole looked at the page. Under the first notes sat a small p. Later there was an f, then another p, then f again. He had assumed the letters were leftover printing or maybe fingering advice, but doorbells didn't lie. He looked at the sheet music Hunter's cousin had left on the piano, then at a different book on the shelf, and noticed the same letters migrating through every piece, always in the same two shapes.

"I wonder if they mean something," Cole said, more to himself than to Hunter.

He tried an experiment. Where the page said p, he played loud, and where it said f, he played soft, just flipping them to see if Hunter noticed anything. Hunter dropped his controller. "Okay, that was weird. It sounded backwards. Do it the other way."

So Cole flipped his flip. Where the p appeared, he made his fingers light, barely brushing the keys, and the melody suddenly felt like it was sneaking somewhere. Where the f showed up, he leaned in and let the sound fill the whole basement, and the sneaking turned into arriving. The same notes, the same order, but now the piece had weather in it. His teacher, Ms. Otieno, had told the class last week that music directions came from Italian, and it clicked into place. "Piano," he said slowly. "It means soft. And forte means loud. That's what the letters are."

"Huh," said Hunter. "So the whole world agreed on that?"

" Somebody did, a long time ago." Cole played the first line again, watching the letters like a lens that made the invisible parts of the music show up. The soft parts were soft on purpose, and the loud parts were loud on purpose, and the difference between them was the whole point. It wasn't a mistake in the printing. It was the map.

By quarter to five he had run the piece six times, and each time the switch from p to f landed cleaner, like a breath he was learning to place. Hunter's dad called down that they should wrap up, and Cole played the last line once more, soft, then loud, then soft again, and held the final note until it thinned into the hum of the furnace.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
Aiden slapped the basketball against the cracked court, caught it, and spun toward the chain-link fence where Paige and Emanuel were waiting with water bottles and Ms. Taylor's old stopwatch. "Two laps around the park loop," he announced. "That's the whole race. Eight hundred metres, and the loop is four hundred, so it's exactly two laps, first lap and second lap, just like a real track." Emanuel groaned the way he always did when Aiden had a plan, but he was already stretching, which meant yes.

The tryouts were on Saturday, and Aiden wanted one thing: to beat his own time from last month. The problem was that every time he ran the loop, he died on the second lap. His legs turned to sand, his lungs burned, and he slowed to a jog before the fence came back into view. "You go out too fast," Paige said, bouncing a ball through the court's crooked hoop between runs. "You look like a rocket for one lap and a snail for the next one." Aiden thought about that. A rocket and a snail averaged out to nothing. Something invisible was stealing his second lap, and he couldn't see it because it happened in the first one.

So he made Saturday's practice a test. Lap one, he would hold back on purpose, keeping his legs quick but easy, even if it felt embarrassingly slow. Lap two, he would let everything go. "That's your plan?" Emanuel said. "Start slow on purpose?" "It's not slow," Aiden said, trying to sound assertive. "It's saved." Ms. Taylor, who was retired and spent half her pension on new running shoes for the neighbourhood kids, had managed to extract a promise from all three of them: no racing the practice, only the real thing. She clicked the stopwatch and said, "Go."

The first lap felt like torture of a completely different kind. His body wanted to fly, and he wouldn't let it. He counted his breathing, watched Paige's sneakers ahead of him, and forced his arms to stay loose. When he crossed the starting line again, that was the halfway mark, and this time he knew it, because four hundred metres meant one lap and one lap meant half the race. He kicked. His legs, unbelievably, still had something in them. He passed Emanuel on the far curve, heard Ms. Taylor shouting something from the basketball court, and sprinted the last stretch so hard he nearly ran into the fence.

He bent over, gasping and laughing at the same time. Paige read the watch and shrieked. "Eleven seconds faster! Eleven!" Emanuel clapped him on the back and demanded they all go again, and Aiden was already lining up at the crack in the pavement where every lap began. "Same plan," he said, toes behind the line. "Watch lap one, then watch me fly."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah reader follows the words with a yad, a pointer whose name means hand, so that the parchment itself is not touched.
story:
Mathis stood in his grandmother's living room with a photocopied page of Hebrew in his hand, and everyone at the family gathering kept asking him the same question. "So you'll read it at your bar mitzvah, sweetie?" said one great-aunt, and "Are you nervous?" said another, and finally his cousin Delaney said, "Can you do it yet or should we all start humming to cover for you?"

"I can do it," Mathis said, though the truth was more complicated. He had been practicing with Mr. Walker, who met him at the kitchen table every Tuesday, and Mr. Walker kept saying the same thing: don't just memorize the sounds, know where you are on the page. At home Mathis had tried to decompose the portion into small chunks, six words at a time, then stitched the chunks together, but whenever he lost his place his mind went blank. His intuition told him the problem wasn't his memory. It was that he had never actually seen the words where they really lived, on the scroll itself, in the strange letters without vowels.

The scroll was at the synagogue, though, and the gathering was here, so Mathis did the next best thing. He made Auguste hold the photocopied page while he recited, and every time he finished a phrase he tapped the paper with his finger to keep his place. "Stop tapping," Auguste said. "You're going to wear a hole through it and then we'll have to tape it and that's embarrassing for both of us." Mathis kept tapping anyway, because the tapping worked. He got through four lines without stopping, and Delaney, who had been eating crackers on the couch like it was a spectator sport, actually applauded with synthetic cheese dust still on her fingers.

At the next Tuesday lesson, Mathis recited for Mr. Walker from memory, finger rising toward the open scroll on the table out of pure habit. Before his fingertip reached the parchment, Mr. Walker slid a slim silver pointer across the table to him. "Use the yad," he said. "It means hand." Mathis took it. The silver finger at the end slid along under the letters, and suddenly the words weren't a chant in his head anymore. They were a place on the page, line after line, and his eyes knew exactly where to land next.

He ran through the whole portion once, slowly, then again faster, and he only wobbled twice. "Better," Mr. Walker said, which from him was a parade. Mathis grinned and kept the yad moving. "Do you think they'd let me keep this for the actual day?" he asked. "In case my finger gets ideas?"

"Your finger," Mr. Walker said, "is on its own from here."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark.
story:
Muhammad lined up seven jars on Mr. Moose's workbench, each one labeled in his careful handwriting: lemon juice, soap water, vinegar, baking soda mix, cola, milk, mystery. Mr. Moose had said he could use the garage every Saturday as long as he monitored the space heater and didn't spill anything on the drill press. The mystery jar was the whole point. Zack had brought it from his kitchen in a jam jar with no label and refused to say what was inside, which was exactly the kind of thing Zack did.

"Loser tests the mystery jar last," Zack said, sitting on an overturned bucket. He wanted the whole thing to be a competition, because Zack wanted everything to be a competition. "Winner gets my dessert on Monday."

"Fine," Muhammad said, though his real want was simpler: Mr. Moose had promised him the old chemistry set on the top shelf if he could prove he knew how to use it properly. Muhammad dipped a strip of litmus paper into the lemon juice and watched it turn pink. Acid. He wrote the result in his notebook, then dipped a fresh strip into the soap water. It went blue. Base. He drew a line down the middle of his page and kept sorting, jar by jar, the way his older sister sorted laundry into two piles.

Halfway through, Zack leaned over and poked the little packet of strips. "This stuff looks like paper. Where do they even get paper that changes color?"

Muhammad read the back of the packet and stopped. "It says here litmus is a dye extracted from lichens," he said. "You know, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark."

"Lichens," Zack repeated, like the word had personally insulted him. "You mean the stuff on my grandpa's garden wall? We've been wiping mystery wall crust on jam juice?"

Muhammad laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the cola. "It's not crust on the paper, it's dye from the crust. There's a difference." He steadied the jar and dipped the strip. Pink, but only a little, a pale rose instead of the deep red the vinegar had given. He wrote that down too, thinking that each liquid had its own strength, sitting somewhere along the scale instead of just picking a team.

Only the mystery jar remained. Zack rubbed his hands together like a cartoon villain. Muhammad dipped the strip, and nothing happened. Paper stayed the same purplish brown. He tried a second strip, then a third, all in vain. "It's water," Muhammad said finally. "Plain water. It's right near the middle, so it doesn't push the paper either way."

Zack's face fell a full inch. "It's my grandma's fancy alkaline water. She pays six dollars a bottle. I was going to watch it blow your mind."

Muhammad tapped the notebook. "Test it yourself." Zack grabbed a strip, jammed it in, and stared at the unchanged paper as the heater ticked in the corner. "Six dollars," he said, "for the median of everything."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Ritardando, often written rit., means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means gradually speeding up.
story:
The church basement smelled of coffee and old hymnals, and Naomi had exactly four days to learn the offertory piece before Sunday. Ms. Zhou, who ran the music program, had marked up the sheet music in red pencil before handing it over, and Naomi had played it through once, twice, three times without understanding what the marks were for. At the top of the second page, in small letters above the staff, sat the word rit.

"You're playing it fine," said Noor, who was folding programs at the far table. Brayden nodded along from the piano bench beside her, humming the melody. That was the problem. It sounded fine. It sounded flat.

On Thursday the three of them tried it as a trio, Naomi on the piano, Noor on flute, Brayden with his trumpet. Sunlight came through the high windows and saturated the worn red carpet, and the sound rose up toward the wooden canopy of the ceiling beams. They started strong. Then, at the second page, something came apart. Naomi heard it before she could name it: Noor's flute line drifted behind, dragging like a boat with a heavy anchor, while Brayden's trumpet charged ahead, bright and buoyant, sailing right over her.

"Hold on," Naomi said, stopping. "We're not together."

"We were together," Brayden insisted. "You slowed down."

"I did not." But she looked down at her hands, wondering. She had played the notes in time. She was almost sure.

Noor traced her finger along her own music. "I slowed down too. Look, the red letters. rit. I asked my cousin, and she said that mark means gradually slowing down." She tapped the page. "That's why I got slower. It's written right there."

Naomi stared at the word. Then she looked at Brayden's sheet, and her stomach dipped. His copy was an older printout, and the tiny marking wasn't there at all. That was it. That was the whole problem. Half the trio had the instruction and half didn't. The music says rit., so the players slow together; his page doesn't, so he keeps the beat.

"Your music is missing the rit.," she said. "It's not you. It's your page."

Brayden held his sheet up to the window and squinted. "There's a smudge. I think it printed light." He grinned. "So I'm not bad, I'm just blind."

They photocopied a clean page from Noor's book, and Ms. Zhou found them a fresh printout with all the markings, including an accelerando near the end that none of them had noticed before. "That one," Noor said, "means gradually speeding up. My cousin drilled me." They ran it again, and this time the slowdown at measure twenty-four felt like a wave settling, and the final speeding-up lifted them all together, three instruments leaning into the same current.

Sunday morning, with the congregation quiet and the light slanting across the altar, Naomi lifted her hands to the keys and glanced at Noor and Brayden. "Measure twenty-four," she whispered. "Ready?"

Brayden raised his trumpet and winked. "Slow and steady."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: Some writers order their points from weakest to strongest, so the argument builds and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason.
story:
Jade slid her notebook across the library table so Trinity and Mohamed-Amine could see the mess inside. Three reasons for her thesis statement sat in a scrambled list, each one crossed out and rewritten twice, and Mr. Marino would collect outlines from the writing club in fifteen minutes. "My thesis is fine," she said. "Schools should start later. It's the three points that are fighting me."

Mohamed-Amine leaned over the list. "Stronger grades, fewer sleepy bus rides, fewer grumpy mornings. Just pick an order." He said it like it was nothing, like the order didn't matter at all, and Jade felt her stomach tighten because she had a secret: she had already ordered them, best first, and something about it felt wrong.

Trinity tapped the page. "Wait. Who told you to put your best reason first?" Jade hadn't told anyone that. "Nobody," she said slowly. "It just seemed smart. Hit them hard, right at the top." Trinity shook her head and pulled out a battered handout from an old debate unit, folded so many times it was soft as cloth. She smoothed it flat and pointed to one line, and Jade read it three times before she let herself believe it. Some writers order their points from weakest to strongest, so the argument builds and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason.

"So the grumpy mornings go first," Jade said, already budgeting her remaining ten minutes, "the bus rides second, and grades last. The reader climbs up instead of downhill." She copied the outline fast, her pen scratching loud in the quiet room, and the order felt like a lock clicking shut. When Mr. Marino came down the row collecting papers, he paused at her page longer than at anyone else's. "Interesting," he said. "Most students front-load their best evidence."

"That's what I thought too," Jade said, watching his face for the verdict. He wrote something at the bottom of her outline and moved on, and she had to wait, hands flat on the table, until he reached the front of the room. Then he held up her paper. "This one builds," he told the club, and his praise was brief but vigorous, the kind that made everyone turn and look. Later, walking out with Trinity, Jade grinned. "Okay, but here's the twist. My best reason was never the grades." Trinity frowned. "It's on your outline. Grades, last, strongest." Jade shrugged, zipping her bag. "The strongest reason is that kids would actually come to school awake. I found it while I was rearranging. It wasn't even on the list until five minutes before he collected it."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: The Galápagos finches have beaks suited to different foods, such as thin beaks for picking insects and deep, heavy beaks for cracking hard seeds.
story:
The trouble started on the nature trail behind school, where Mr. Hernández had set up a folding table beside the poison ivy sign. On the table sat a shoebox labeled FINCH MODELS, DO NOT DROP, and next to it two trays: one of hard little seeds and one of dead insects that had expired some time ago and smelled like it. Natalie's presentation on natural selection was due Friday, and Mr. Hernández had said, cheerfully, that she would "discover it herself" on the trail, which sounded like something a person says when they own a box of dead insects.

"So the birds all came from the same ancestor," Yusuf said, picking up a model with a thin, delicate beak, "and then each island gave them different food, and the beaks that matched survived." He said it the way he said everything, like he was reading it off the back of his hand. Natalie had read the same page four times and still could not make the shapes in her head move the right way.

"They're migratory," Bronson offered from a log, where he was excavating a granola bar from the bottom of his backpack one layer at a time. "The birds. Probably." Nobody confirmed this, and Bronson did not require confirmation.

Natalie lined the models up anyway, because she had an idea she could test: match each beak to its food and see if the matching made sense. The thin beak she held over the insect tray, and it slid neatly between the legs of a dead beetle, the way tweezers would. Then she picked up the deep, heavy beak, the one shaped like a pair of pliers, and pressed it down on a hard seed. The seed cracked. She tried the thin beak on the same seed and got nothing but a seed with a very clean dent. She tried the heavy beak on the insect and squashed it flat, which the insect arguably deserved.

That night Yusuf texted her a picture of his own kitchen table, covered in cracked sunflower seeds and a binder clip he had labeled as a stand-in for the heavy beak. "broke 3 clips," the message read. "mom wants to know why. told her natural selection. she said clean it up." Natalie screenshotted it for slide nine.

On Friday she stood at the front of the room with the two models and both trays. "Thin beaks for picking insects," she said, holding one up, "deep, heavy beaks for cracking hard seeds." She set the heavy model down on a seed, and it split with a sound like a small knuckle cracking.

"That," said Bronson, from the back, "is the best noise this class has ever made."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
story:
Blake's aunt's kitchen smelled of cinnamon and chopped pecans, and his cousin Giuliana sat at the table with a paper so creased it looked like an old map. She was thirteen and a half, but in six months she would turn fifteen, and her whole family was already talking about it.

"I have to say the reading at the Mass," Giuliana said, pushing the paper toward him. "The quinceañera, my fifteenth birthday, it starts with the Mass of thanksgiving, and I have to stand up in front of everybody and not mess up."

Blake picked up the paper. The words were from the prophet Isaiah, about not being afraid, and Giuliana had underlined three lines so hard the pen had torn through. "You've got six months," he said. "That's plenty."

"That's what my mom said. Then she said her cousin froze at hers and had to be whispered through it, and everybody still talks about it." Giuliana rested her chin on her fist. "The problem is I only know it when I'm calm, sitting here. Church won't be calm."

Blake thought about that. She wasn't struggling with the words themselves; she was struggling with what would happen when the setting changed. The problem was invisible, hiding somewhere between her memory and her nerves, so he couldn't just watch for it. He needed a way to make it show itself.

"Okay," he said slowly. "What if practicing here isn't the real test, because here nothing can go wrong? We need to make things go wrong on purpose, a little bit at a time, and see what breaks." He went to the junk drawer, found a bag of dried beans, and poured a handful on the table. "Every time you finish a line, I drop a bean in a metal bowl. If you can keep going through the noise, you can keep going through a cough or a crying baby."

Giuliana laughed, which was already something. She started the reading, and Blake waited until the trickiest underlined line, then clacked the bean down right in the middle of it. She stumbled, glared at him, and kept going. He dropped two at once. She kept going. Then he stood on a chair and dropped one from ceiling height, and the crash it made was so ridiculous that she laughed mid-sentence, lost her place, and had to feel her way back.

"There," Blake said. "See, the fear isn't that you'll forget. It's that you'll think one stumble means it's over. But you found your way back just now without any help."

"You dropped beans on me from the ceiling," she said.

"Ten beans from one bag. And I'll do it again tomorrow, and the day after." He gathered them up. "Eventually the noise won't mean anything, because you'll have survived it, like, thirty times."

They practiced until the light outside went orange, and when Giuliana's mother called them for dinner, Giuliana folded the paper and slid it into her back pocket instead of leaving it on the table. At dinner she recited the whole first paragraph from memory while Blake dropped his fork loudly on his plate, and she never stopped, not even when her little brother applauded with his mouth full.

"Tomorrow," she whispered to Blake as they cleared the plates, "bring the big pot."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Motion sickness happens when the eyes and the balance organs in the inner ear send the brain conflicting signals about whether the body is moving.
story:
The van had barely left their street when Nolan opened his book, and by the third switchback on the hill road his stomach had turned against him completely. He remembered it now with his forehead pressed against the cool glass of the airport window: his mother pulling over, the taste of the roadside air, the paperback lying shut on the seat for the rest of the drive.

"You look like somebody stole your birthday," said Lennox, who had ridden to the airport with them to see Nolan off. Alora stood beside him, spinning her keychain lanyard in tight circles.

"I got sick in the van," Nolan said. "From reading. And now I have to get on a plane for six hours, and I want to read this book so bad I could die." He held it up, a fat fantasy with a cracked spine, the one he'd been saving for the trip.

Alora stopped spinning the lanyard. "My cousin says it's called motion sickness. It happens when your eyes and the balance organs in your inner ear send your brain conflicting signals about whether your body is moving." She shrugged. "She read it off a poster at the clinic."

Nolan turned that over. His eyes, glued to a still page, had been telling his brain nothing was moving, while the winding road had been throwing his inner ear all over the place. Two witnesses giving opposite testimony. He had been sick in the middle of the disagreement.

"So it's not the driving," he said slowly. "It's the mismatch."

"Okay, scientist," Lennox said, but he was grinning.

They found seats near the departures board, and Nolan spread his snack crackers like lab equipment. The moving walkway ran past them, a smooth river of carpet. "Watch," he said. He stepped on with the book open and his eyes down, and rode it two lengths. His stomach grumbled, uneasy but not mutinous. Then he rode it looking up at the ceiling instead, and the queasy feeling faded to almost nothing.

"So the fix is to make the two signals agree," Alora said, picking up a cracker. "Look out the window on the plane, don't look at the page."

"That's the problem." Nolan gazed at his book, at the paperback he had guarded through a month of homework. "The whole reason I brought it."

Mr. Kamau, the neighbour who had helped carry the suitcases, settled onto the bench beside them. "Boarding soon, I think. The line at Gate 14 is dissolving already."

Nolan watched the queue shrink. It was the family's first big trip in years, and he wanted to remember every minute of it, but he could already see the trade: the window seat and the wide sky, or the story waiting on page three hundred. The consensus at the departure board was that Flight 882 was on time, and that was final.

He zipped the book into his backpack, right down at the bottom, under the socks.

"For when we land," he said.

Lennox clapped his shoulder once, hard. "Bring back the ending at least."

"Every word of it," Nolan said, and lifted his bag toward the gate.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: In the absorption method, rice cooks in a measured amount of water that it soaks up completely, so no water needs to be drained.
story:
Riley stood in the middle of her uncle's restaurant kitchen on a Saturday morning, holding a clipboard with three circles drawn on it and a pot of rice about to boil over. Raymond leaned against the stainless steel counter, eating a pickle he had definitely stolen from the sandwich station. "You're supposed to be learning to cook," he said. "That's the analysis," Riley said, tapping the clipboard. "Curry takes twenty minutes, rice takes fifteen, and flatbread takes two minutes per piece, so if I work backwards, the rice should be my alarm clock." Lyvia, who had already burned one flatbread into something resembling a fossil, raised her spatulan in salute. "Your alarm clock is beeping," she said.

The rice pot began to gurgle like a small angry frog. Riley peered at it, frowned, and grabbed the colander. She was halfway to the sink, pot tilted, when Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya, the chef whose actual job this kitchen was, appeared beside her like a very calm ghost. "Stop," he said. "Where are you going with my rice?" Riley blinked. "To drain it? Like pasta?" He shook his head and pointed at the measuring cup still sitting by the stove. "This is the absorption method. The rice cooks in a measured amount of water that it soaks up completely. All of it. There's nothing left to drain."

Riley looked into the pot. The water had vanished, absorbed somewhere into the grains, and the rice sat there looking plump and smug, like it had eaten the whole lake and hidden the evidence. "So if I'd drained it," she said slowly, "I would have poured out..." "Nothing," said Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya. "And also my foot, probably, so thank you for stopping." Raymond snickered into his pickle.

She carried the pot back to the stove and adjusted her clipboard. The curry was bubbling, the flatbread dough was resting under a cloth, and the rice just needed to sit, off the heat, doing its secret invisible work. That was the part she liked, the hidden part, water going in and disappearing, timing you couldn't watch happen. She counted backward again. Curry, then flatbread, then lift the lid.

The flatbread puffed up on the hot pan like it was taking a deep breath, and when Lyvia's second attempt didn't burn, the whole kitchen stopped smelling faintly toxic and started smelling like actual dinner. Raymond abandoned his pickle without ceremony. "Plate," Riley ordered, sliding the lid off the rice at last, fluffy and complete, not a drop drained away. Raymond held out a plate and saluted with the other hand. "At your service, chef. Rice, curry, bread, all at the same time." Riley looked at the three dishes, hot together, and said, "You may carry the clipboard."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Tropical rainforests lie near the equator, where strong sunlight heats moist air that rises, cools and forms clouds, often bringing heavy afternoon rain.
story:
Sydney spread the two graphs across her knees as Ms. Mercer's truck climbed onto the plateau, the desert flattening into brown silence on every side. One graph showed rainfall and temperature for a desert; the other showed the same for a tropical rainforest. Her assignment was to compare them, but the rainforest graph looked wrong to her. "Who gets twenty-five centimetres of rain in a single month?" she muttered.

Forrest leaned over from the middle seat, holding his phone against the bumps in the road. "My aunt. She's in the Amazon right now." He scrolled through her photos. "Look, blue sky every single morning." He swiped again. "And then, every afternoon, this." The photo showed a wall of grey rain hammering a tin roof, lightning forked over the trees.

"That can't be right," Sydney said. "If it storms every afternoon, why is it always clear in the morning?" She frowned at the phone, then at her graphs, then at the window, where the sun was climbing higher and the rocks outside had started to shimmer. She remembered last summer, sitting on the dock at the lake with her dad, how the morning would be glassy and still and then, around three o'clock, clouds would pile up and thunder would roll in off the water. She had always blamed the clouds on the day "turning bad." Now she turned the idea over like a stone. The rainforest sat near the equator, where the sun was strongest. Strong sunlight heated the moist air, the air rose, cooled, and formed clouds, and the clouds brought heavy afternoon rain. It was a cycle you could almost set your watch by.

"So the mornings aren't lucky," she said slowly. "They're just the first half of the same machine." She grabbed a pencil and drew a curve across the rainforest graph, peaking in the afternoon. "That's why the rainfall bars cluster there. And the desert," she tapped her other graph, "hardly gets any of this at all. Look at the temperature line, though. It swings wild, hot days, cold nights, because there's no cloud cover." The comparison she'd planned, hottest place wins, suddenly seemed too simple, and she crossed out her first paragraph.

"Hey," Forrest said, squinting at his phone. "My aunt sent these out of order. Check the timestamps." Sydney leaned in. Half the "morning" photos were actually taken after the storms had cleared, near sunset. She laughed, shaking her head. She'd been ready to argue with the photos.

They stopped at a frugal little gas station where Ms. Mercer bought one giant soda and three straws, and they drank it under the awning while the afternoon heat invaded every shady corner. Sydney looked out at the bleached horizon and thought of the Amazon, where at this very hour the rain would be slamming down. "Same sun," she said. "Different air." Forrest raised his straw in a toast to the equator.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
story:
The number 42 bus rattled past the bakery on Fifth Street, and Wyatt held his phone close so the glare from the window would not wash out the screen. He was watching a video of Dash Merrill, a famous streamer, holding up the new AeroCourt sneakers and saying they were the best shoes he had ever laced up. Wyatt wanted those shoes so badly his ribs felt tight. His old pair had a hole along the sole, and tryouts for the travel team were in three weeks.

Kylan leaned over from the seat beside him. "You're getting those, right? Half the team already has them."

"Trace got his yesterday," Wyatt said. "He said everybody who's anybody is wearing Aeros."

Kylan nodded like that settled it. Wyatt thumbed back to the top of the video to watch it again, and this time he noticed the caption underneath. Tucked between the fire emojis, almost hidden, were two small characters: #ad. He stopped the video with his thumb.

"Wait," he said. "It says ad." He scrolled to another Dash Merrill video from last month, one where Dash praised a sports drink. The caption there read, "Thanks to the brand for sending this to me for free!" Wyatt sat back against the hard plastic seat. In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission makes influencers disclose when they got paid or got free stuff to promote something, he remembered Mr. Lewandowski mentioning in media class before spring break, back when Wyatt had half listened. If Dash truly loved the shoes, would he need a tag hiding in the caption?

"I'm going to test something," Wyatt said. He watched three more Dash videos. The ones with #ad or "free product" in the caption were the ones where Dash used loaded words like "incredible" and "revolutionary" over and over. The ones with no tag, where Dash was just playing games and grumbling about lag, sounded like a regular person. The pattern held every single time.

"So maybe Dash's motivation is the money, not the shoes," Wyatt said slowly.

Kylan frowned at the paused screen. "So Trace got fooled?"

"Trace got persuading," Wyatt said. "Ads do it on purpose. They pile on the famous person, the everybody-has-it thing, the amazing-incredible words, until you can't think straight." He looked down at his own shoes, the holey, mud-crusted ones. His mom had said the budget was tight this month, that things were a little impoverished until her next paycheck, and he had felt embarrassed when she said it. Now he was almost glad. He had almost spent two months of saved allowance on a shoe a stranger was paid to praise.

At his stop, Wyatt pocketed the phone and stepped down into the afternoon heat. His old shoes compressed against the pavement with each step, soft and familiar. He would wear them to tryouts, hole and all.

"Catch you tomorrow," Kylan called through the window as the bus hissed away. "And tell Trace to look for the little tag!"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green, and mixing two complementary paints produces a dull brown or gray.
story:
Raphael spread his paints across the kitchen table and propped up the poster board Ms. Lavoie had appointed him to paint for the class concert backdrop. He had volunteered for the sunset scene, imagining streaks of orange and red over a dark green hillside. His first attempt lay beside him, drying into the color of puddles.

"You've done that three times," Adelle said from across the table, dipping her brush into blue for her part of the project, a train crossing under the sunset. "It keeps coming out brown."

"I know." Raphael frowned at the muddy hill. He had started with bright red for the sky, then brushed green over the hill where the two shapes met. Each time, the line between them turned a dull grayish brown, no matter how carefully he worked. He wondered if his brushes were dirty, so he washed them in the jar of water until it clouded pink, then tried again on a scrap of paper. Clean brush, red stroke, green stroke beside it. Where they touched, brown.

He pulled out the little cardboard color wheel from his pencil case, the one with the spinning disk, and turned it slowly. Red sat on one side, green exactly opposite it. He spun the disk again to be sure, because it seemed strange that two colors so far apart could ruin each other.

"Hey, Adelle. Red and green are opposite each other on the color wheel. I think they're complementary colors."

"So?"

"So every time my red sky touches my green hill, it goes muddy." He tested it, dragging red into green on the scrap and watching the brown bloom, then dragging red into blue instead, which stayed rich and purple-dark. It was the green. He cut a thin strip of paper, laid it along the bottom of his board, and penciled a hill on it, then painted the hill green up to the strip, and the red sky above, so the two paints never touched. When the strip came away, the sunset blazed down to a clean edge, the hill below it deep and cool.

Albert arrived with his backpack still on, holding the model train he had built for the conductor figure Ms. Lavoie wanted painted beside the crossing. He stopped in the doorway.

"Whoa. That actually looks like a sunset."

Raphael held up the muddy scrap of paper next to the finished board. "Complementary colors," he said. "Opposites on the wheel. Keep them apart or they turn brown."

"Then my blue better not touch your orange," Adelle said, edging her railroad crossing toward the edge of the board.

"It won't," Raphael said, and slid the poster gently toward the window, where the frail afternoon light caught the red sky and made it glow.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: In the dark, the eyes slowly grow more sensitive as rod cells in the retina rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, which takes half an hour or more.
story:
The power died right in the middle of the courtroom show Grandpa had been watching, and the whole house went black in one blink. "Right when the defendant was about to testify," Grandpa groaned, feeling along the arm of his chair. "Forty years I've watched that program, and the lights pick tonight to quit."

Louis held his hand in front of his face and could barely find it, just a pale smear where his fingers should have been. He edged toward the kitchen for the flashlight, knocking his hip on the doorframe on the way, and his grandfather laughed so hard he wheezed. "Slow down, Louis. Nothing in this old house has moved since 1987."

But that was the thing. The house hadn't moved, and Louis still couldn't see it. He found the flashlight in the junk drawer, but when he clicked it, nothing happened. He shook it, clicked again, and unscrewed the cap to scrutinize the inside. The batteries were crusted white and green at the ends, dead as fossils. He tried the batteries from the remote, then from the clock radio, lining them up on the counter in a systematic row, testing each one. None of them worked either.

Then Meadow banged on the front door, having seen the dark from across the street. She came in with her phone, but she was saving its charge, so they all sat in the living room without it, and Louis said, "Watch this. I'm doing an experiment." He held up his hand again. Still almost nothing. "Ten minutes ago I couldn't even see my fingers. Let's see what happens if we just wait."

They played a guessing game in the dark, naming what they thought was in front of them, and Grandpa kept score and lost track twice. After a while Meadow said, "Wait, I can see the bookshelf. Like, actually see it." Louis stood up and walked, slowly, all the way around the coffee table without touching it once, and he made it to the window and back. His eyes had somehow rebuilt whatever it was they needed, right there in the dark.

"How," Meadow demanded.

Grandpa leaned forward. "Rhodopsin," he said, and tapped the side of his eye. "Give it half an hour."

Meadow turned her phone on and checked the time. "Louis, it's been thirty-three minutes." Louis threw both fists in the air, shadowy against the grey of the window, and crowed, "Right on schedule!"

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there.
story:
Madison pressed her pencil so hard against the ruler that the graphite snapped. The assignment on the board read "One-Point Perspective: A Street," and Mr. Oyelaran had drawn a dot in the middle of his example and labeled it vanishing point. Every line in his street, the curbs, the rooflines, the shop windows, ran back to that dot. But every time Madison tried it, her street looked like it was sliding sideways down the page, like a rudder had caught the current and turned the whole town.

"Yours is crooked," said Rylan, leaning over from the next table. "Mine's crooked too, but yours is worse."

"Thanks." Madison erased her lines until the paper went translucent in one gray patch. She wanted this drawing to work, because her mom had promised to frame something for the hallway at home, and she did not want to frame a melting street.

Mr. Oyelaran walked between the tables. "The old painters used strings," he said on his way past, not stopping. "Think about that." Then he was gone, and Madison frowned at the back of his shirt. Strings? She copied his words into the margin of her sketchbook so she would not lose them.

At lunch she found Alisa in the library, because Alisa read art books for fun. "Strings," Madison said. "Mr. Oyelaran said the old painters used strings, and I don't know what that means, but my street keeps tilting."

Alisa pulled a big book off the shelf and opened it flat between them. "Look at this one. The Last Supper." The painting stretched across two pages, the long table, the thirteen figures, the windows behind them pale like translucent panes of light. "Here's the part that goes with strings," Alisa said, tapping the caption with one finger. "In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there."

Madison bent close. There, small and dark, a tiny hole sat right at the head, and when she laid her pencil along the edges of the ceiling beams, the table, the tapestries, they all fell toward it, every one. She tried it from the other side too, and again the lines obeyed. "He put the point on the most important thing in the whole picture," she said slowly. "Everything leads your eye there. And the strings held the lines straight, like a rudder holding a course, so the room wouldn't tilt."

That afternoon she started over. She made her dot, then, because she had no string, she poked a pin through the paper at the point and fished thread through it, holding the thread taut with one hand and drawing along it with the other. Line by line her street straightened and locked into place. Rylan came over and stood silent for a moment. "Okay," he said. "Yours is better than mine now."

On Friday Mr. Oyelaran held her drawing up in front of the class. "Notice," he said, "how every line obeys the point." He turned it toward the window, and the light shone straight through the little pinhole in the middle, so that the street appeared to run toward a shining sun. "You've got a hole in your paper, Madison," he said, peering closer. "But I have to admit, it's the best mistake on this wall."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.
story:
Ivy pulled on a pair of plastic gloves and stood at the sorting table between Ana and Alexia. Behind them, shelves of donated cans rose to the ceiling, and in front of them lay a mountain of grocery bags still waiting to be unpacked.

"Check every date," said Mr. Ramírez, walking past with a clipboard. "Anything expired goes in the toss bin."

Ivy opened the first bag and pulled out a box of oat cereal. The date on the top flap read one day earlier than today's date. She held it over the bin, then stopped. It seemed strange that a sealed box would go bad overnight, like a switch flipping at midnight.

"Alexia, look at this," she said. "It just says 'best if used by.' It doesn't say expires."

Alexia leaned over. "Mr. Ramírez said expired stuff goes out."

"But this doesn't say expired." Ivy turned the box over in her hands. "It says best. Like, the company thinks it tastes best by yesterday. That's not the same as unsafe." She set the box aside and dug through three more bags, laying out every item with a date. Most said "best if used by." One jar of pickles said "use by." She made two piles and counted. Eleven boxes were one or two days past their dates, and every single one was sealed.

Ana came over and frowned at the piles. "You're keeping the old stuff?"

"I'm testing an idea. I think the words mean different things." Ivy raised her hand as Mr. Ramírez passed again. "Can I ask about dates? What's the difference between 'best if used by' and 'use by'?"

He picked up the cereal box and squinted at it. "That one's a quality date. In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date."

"So the cereal's still fine?"

"For a food bank, yes. Cereal, pasta, canned goods, we can use all of that past the date. Now the pickles, we'll check those separately." He moved on to the next table.

Ivy slid the eleven boxes back into the keep pile. "There's an irony here," she said. "People probably donated these because they thought they were spoiled. If they'd known, they might have eaten them themselves."

"Or the stores couldn't sell them," Ana said, stacking the cereal on a shelf. "Conventional grocery stores won't put anything past its date out front, even if it's fine."

By the end of the shift, the shelves had filled enough to sustain the whole week of pickups. Mr. Ramírez handed out paper cups of apple juice and held up his clipboard. "Ivy, you caught the date thing. I'm putting you on sorting every Saturday."

"Both piles?" she asked.

"Both piles," he said, and drew a smiley face next to her name.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
Mackenzie set her fork down and pushed the meatloaf around her plate. She had been quiet since she walked in the door, and her mother noticed before the second helping was served.

"You failed a quiz," her mother guessed. "You broke something."

"Worse." Mackenzie stared at the glass of milk. "Ariya snubbed me after school. Walked right past me in the hall. I said hi twice and she didn't even look up. So I told Dakota she's stuck up, and now half the class thinks so too."

Her father reached for the salt. "Half an hour before that, maybe?"

"How would you know?"

"I wouldn't. I'd speculate." He shrugged. "That's the point of guessing instead of deciding."

Mackenzie rolled her eyes, but the question stuck to her all through dinner. Afterward she went upstairs and opened her laptop. She had a social studies assignment due anyway, so she told herself she was just avoiding it when she typed why do people assume things about other people into the search bar. One result, from a psychology site, made her stop chewing the last of her gum. In 1977, a psychologist named Lee Ross called it the fundamental attribution error: the tendency to blame other people's actions on their personality while underestimating their situation. She read the sentence three times.

Her phone buzzed. Dakota: did u hear about Ariya?? She got the callback list. Lead role went to someone else. Cried in the bathroom 6th period.

Mackenzie sat very still. Ariya had been carrying the news about the audition the whole day, probably since before the hallway, probably since the list went up outside the drama room at lunch. Mackenzie had watched a girl stare at the floor and read a personality instead. She scrolled back through the messages she had sent Dakota. Stuck up. Thinks she's too good. The words looked obsolete now, like something from an old textbook that had been corrected.

She typed a reply. we have to fix this. Then she started drafting something longer, to Ariya. She deleted it twice because it kept sounding like an apology for a thing she couldn't name without making it worse. On the third try she kept it to two lines: I heard about the list. I should have asked if you were okay instead of deciding you weren't.

She sent it before she could delete it again, then pulled on her jacket. There was a game night at the community center, and both of them always went. If Ariya showed up, Mackenzie would be there first, standing near the door with the good seats already saved.

Her phone buzzed once more as she reached the sidewalk. Coming, it said.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: With Grade in Rows, Answer in Columns and Answer again in Values as a count, a pivot table shows how many students in each grade gave each answer.
story:
John sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a laptop and a problem. The student council had surveyed the whole school about moving lunch thirty minutes later, and tomorrow morning Mr. Moretti would announce the results at assembly. John had promised to have the breakdown by grade ready tonight, but the spreadsheet held four hundred rows of answers and no obvious pattern.

"I don't get it," Deacon said, leaning over his shoulder. "Just count them. How long can it take?"

"You count them," Oscar said. "I did thirty rows before lunch and I wanted to lie down."

Their arguing had already made John the one who mediated between them in science class, and he did it again now without thinking. "Oscar counts, Deacon writes the totals. I'll keep looking for a better way." He scrolled through the survey answers, noticing that the same two columns repeated everywhere: Grade, and Answer, which was either "Yes, later lunch" or "No, keep it now."

Grandpa shuffled in with two mugs of tea and set one beside the mouse. "Still fighting about lunch? When I was your age we fought about important things, like the mortgage on a leaky roof." He tapped the window frame, where rain had swelled the wood. "Porous old house. Drinks water like a camel." Then he peered at the screen. "What's that Insert tab for? Never seen a program with so many buttons."

John clicked it, mostly to answer a question with something better than a shrug, and there it was: PivotTable. He dragged it onto a new sheet and found three empty boxes labeled Filters, Rows, Columns, and Values. He tried dragging Answer into Rows, then Grade into Columns, and got a tangle of zeros.
