Deacon laughed. Oscar said, "Try it backwards." So John dragged Grade into Rows and Answer into Columns, and the table rebuilt itself, still mostly blank.

"Needs something in Values," Grandpa said, pointing with a knuckle.

John dragged Answer into the Values box too, the same field, twice, and set it to count. The table filled like frost spreading across glass. Rows of grades down the side, the two answers across the top, and where they crossed, actual counts. In grade 6, forty-one said no and nine said yes. Grade 8 flipped completely: sixty-two yes, eleven no. Grade 7 was nearly split. The whole school had voted yes by a hair, but the grades wanted opposite things.

"So it's the eighth graders pushing it through," Oscar said slowly, counting down the column with his finger. "The little kids mostly hate it."

"Then Mr. Moretti should know that before he announces it," John said. "A total hides this." He copied the table, pasted it into an email, and attached the spreadsheet. His message asked whether the council might propose different lunch shifts by grade instead of one change for everyone.

Grandpa carried the mugs to the sink. "Two hundred rows of kids, and one little table tells the truth," he said. "Now come eat before your grandmother decides we're porous too."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: 20/40 vision means you must stand 20 feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from 40 feet.
story:
Amelia had been bragging for three days. "Twenty forty," she announced, holding the optometrist's report above her head like a trophy. "Jenson, you're probably only twenty twenty. Smaller number. Sorry."

Jenson looked up from the kitchen table, where he was supposed to be helping her sort the box of new glasses samples her mom had brought home from the clinic. "Bigger is better," he agreed slowly, "in pizza and in allowance. Probably in eyes too."

Amelia's mom, indifferent to the whole debate, was reading a magazine at the far end of the long hallway. The new glasses sat in their case, still unworn, because Amelia had decided wearing them might make her look like she needed them, which would be embarrassing for someone with such impressive eyes.

They set up an experiment. Amelia copied a line of letters from the report's sample chart and taped it to the kitchen doorframe. Then she paced down the hallway, heel to toe, counting. Twenty feet. She squinted. The letters dissolved into gray smudges, like the TV did when she watched from the couch instead of the good chair.

"Hey Mom," she called. "Can you read the paper on the door?"

Her mom glanced up from her chair near the window. "Sure. E, Z, P, something with a tail, maybe a Q."

Amelia felt something sink. Her mom was way back there, and the doorway looked tiny from this end. She counted on her fingers, twice, because the first answer was annoying. "You're like forty feet away."

"So?" Her mom turned a page.

"So that means twenty forty means I have to stand twenty feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from forty feet." Amelia glared at the smudgy Q. "It's not a score. It's like being graded on a test I keep failing by standing too close to the answers."

Jenson made a noise like a deflating balloon. "So your eyes are the worst thing about you. The very worst."

"Refract somewhere else," Amelia said, pointing at the door, though she wasn't entirely sure that was how eyes worked and suspected Jenson wasn't either.

She walked back up the hallway, opened the glasses case, and put them on. The world snapped into focus so sharply she flinched. The Q was a Q. Her mom had two different socks on. The hallway had a crack in the ceiling she had never once noticed.

And the gray shape that had been shuffling around the backyard for weeks, the one she'd insisted was the neighbor's beautiful fluffy cat? It was a raccoon. It was standing on the picnic table, washing a slice of pizza.

"Jenson," she whispered. "Come look at my cat."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
The sports bar was loud enough that Madison had to lean across the table to hear her uncle at all. On the big screen above the booths, a batter walked, and the crowd on TV cheered while the numbers along the bottom of the screen rolled past like vapor rising off a pot. Her dad pointed at one of the numbers and said the batter was hitting two-eighty, and Madison wondered what that even meant, since the batter had just failed to hit anything.

"What's two-eighty?" she asked.

"How often he gets a hit," her uncle said. "Two hundred eighty hits for every thousand times up. Roughly." He stirred his drink. "Course, there's a guy who wrote a whole book saying everybody was watching the wrong number."

Madison slid her mozzarella stick around the plate. "A whole book about the wrong number?"

"Moneyball," her uncle said. "Michael Lewis, 2003. It's about the Oakland Athletics in 2002. They had almost no money compared to the rich teams, so they couldn't buy the big stars. Instead they used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." He tapped the table. "Players other teams thought weren't worth much."

Madison asked what on-base percentage counted. Her uncle held up a finger. "Times you get on base. Any way at all. A walk counts." He pointed back at the screen. "Like that guy just now. He walked. Your dad's two-eighty says that was nothing. On-base percentage says he did his job."

Madison chewed on that. So the batting average her dad cited all the time was one number standing for hundreds of games, thousands of pitches, and it left some of the good stuff out. A walk got thrown away like it was vapor. She looked at the little stat box in the corner and tried to picture what the number would look like if walks counted too. It would be bigger, she decided. Maybe a lot bigger.

"Okay," she said, "test." She pointed at the shortstop, whose average was said to be terrible, two-ten. "Watch him. If he walks a bunch, the two-ten thing is wrong about him."

"Two-ten is two-ten," her dad said.

"That's naive," Madison said, and immediately worried that was rude, but her uncle laughed so she kept going. "It's only the hits. It doesn't see the walks."

For two innings they watched. The shortstop struck out once, which Madison had to admit supported her dad. Then he fouled off four pitches, worked the count full, and walked. Next time up he walked again, taking a close pitch that the catcher clearly thought was a strike. "See!" Madison grabbed her uncle's arm. "He's getting on base. Every single time. If he does that in every game all season, he's helping more than the guy with the fancy average."

Her uncle pulled out his phone and looked the shortstop up. "Huh," he said, and turned the screen toward her. There it was, a second number beside the first, and it was much kinder to the shortstop.

"Dad," Madison said, holding up a mozzarella stick like a bat, "you owe me an apology on behalf of batting average."

Her dad raised his glass. "I'll never trust a bottom-line number again."

"You will," Madison said. "You'll just read two of them."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: To ask for the bill in a Spanish-speaking restaurant, a customer can say "La cuenta, por favor," meaning "The bill, please."
story:
Brooklyn slid her menu, a laminated sheet of paper, to the edge of the desk that stood perpendicular to Mr. Rowe's long table, which he had draped with a red cloth and set up as "El Restaurante Sol." All week the seventh graders had been practicing food words, and today was the full performance. Clayton wore a paper bow tie and carried a notepad. Haylee had made a cardboard sign that read "Cerrado" on one side and "Abierto" on the other, and she flipped it to "Abierto" with a solemn little flourish.

Brooklyn ordered first, carefully. "Quisiera un sándwich de queso y un jugo de naranja, por favor." Clayton scribbled it down, delivered a plastic sandwich two minutes later, and moved on to the next table of desks. Brooklyn ate her pretend lunch. Then she waited. And waited. She noticed that at every other table, the students were also just sitting there,_menus still open, drumming their fingers, while Clayton circled the room taking new orders but never bringing anything that looked like a check.

She began to reason it out. In a real restaurant, the waiter brought the bill near the end, but here nothing was ending. Maybe the waiters thought everyone was still eating. Or maybe, she thought, a waiter doesn't just know you want the bill. Maybe in Spanish you have to ask for it, the way you ask for food. She couldn't find that phrase anywhere on her vocabulary sheet, which listed el pan, el pollo, la leche, and nothing about paying. She flipped the sheet over. Blank. She glanced at the poster near the window, the one Mr. Rowe kept for fun, full of travel phrases: "¿Dónde está el baño?" and "Buenos días" and, near the bottom, "La cuenta, por favor."

That was it, she decided, or at least worth testing. She raised her hand to catch Clayton's eye and said, clearly, "La cuenta, por favor." Clayton's face brightened. He strode over, tore a sheet from his notepad, wrote a total on it, and presented it with a small bow. At the next table, Haylee watched this, turned to her own customers, and repeated the words, and suddenly bills were appearing all around the room. Mr. Rowe, who planned to retire in two years and had told them he liked saving his energy for after school, gave Brooklyn a slow thumbs-up from his chair in the corner, where he sat at leisure with his coffee mug, letting the class run itself.

Brooklyn counted out the plastic coins in her pouch, paid Clayton, and left them all on the desk as a tip. On her way past the poster, she tapped the line at the bottom twice with her finger. "The bill, please," she murmured to herself, "in case I ever need it."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations have no solution, such as x + 1 = x + 2, because no number is one more and two more than itself at once.
story:
The community centre had turned its back room into a puzzle challenge, with plastic ivy on the walls and a rubber fungus glued to a log in the corner to simulate a forest cave. Mr. Navarro, who ran the Wednesday group, had set out four locked boxes, and each box needed a number for its combination lock. "Solve the equation, punch in the value of x," he said, tapping the card taped to the first box. "Titus's team got box one in nine minutes. Beat that if you can."

Titus wanted the record. He had written his time, 9:12, on the whiteboard by the door and underlined it twice. "Nobody's touching that," he said, arms crossed, watching Daniel and Blake work. Blake picked up the first card and groaned. "It's math homework in disguise. x plus seven equals twelve. Great." He turned the card over, hoping for a hint on the back, and found only a drawing of a beetle.

Daniel took the card. He had been learning equations in class all month, and the rule finally felt solid in his hands: whatever you did to one side, you did to the other. Take away seven from both sides and x stood alone, equal to five. He spun the dial to 5, the lock popped, and Blake made a sound like a kettle. "Okay," Blake said. "Okay, that was actually satisfying." Box two took longer, because the x was trapped on both sides, 3x plus 2 equals x plus ten, and Daniel had to subtract an x from each side before anything else made sense. He narrated each move out loud, and Blake checked it on scrap paper like a co-pilot.

Box three was the one that broke him. The card read x plus 1 equals x plus 2. Daniel subtracted 1 from both sides and got x equals x plus 1. He subtracted x and got 0 equals 1, which made his stomach drop. He punched in 0 anyway. Nothing. He tried 1. Nothing. He tried 5, then 12, then negative 3, spinning the dial faster each time while Titus smirked from the doorway. "Clock's running," Titus sang out. "Eleven minutes."

Daniel stared at the card. He ran the numbers in his head again, and this time he stopped trying to find the answer and looked at what the equation was asking for. A number that was one more than itself and two more than itself. At the same time. He tested the idea with the simplest number he knew: if x was 2, the left side said 3 and the right side said 4. If x was a million, the left side said a million and one, the right a million and two. No number could do both. It wasn't that he hadn't found the answer yet. There wasn't one to find. "It's a trick card," he said slowly. "There's no number that's one more and two more than itself at once. No solution." Blake grabbed the card and squinted at it. "That's not fair," he said, then paused. "Unless..." He flipped the box over. On the bottom, where nobody had looked, a sticker read: if the equation has no solution, turn the key in the small slot. There was a small slot.

Blake turned the key. The box opened on the first try, and inside was a card with the final time and a rubber beetle for the winner. Daniel wrote 13:40 on the whiteboard, well behind Titus, and Titus laughed but clapped him on the shoulder. "Next time I'm taking the trick card first," Titus said, and Blake held up the beetle. "I want a rematch," Blake said. "Same room, same cards. I want to be the one who spots it."

Mr. Navarro collected the cards, smiling at the one that had caused all the trouble. "Four boxes, four locks, and one of them never opens the normal way," he said. Daniel slid the trick card into his pocket to copy later, and Blake was already spinning the dial of box one again, just to feel it pop.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
story:
Simon needed twenty more dollars for the new Aero Swift sneakers, and his mother had said no twice, so he was at the library after school hunting for a way to change her mind. He spread three magazines across the table near the window, each one open to a shoe ad, while Milena dropped her backpack into the chair beside him.

"Same shoes Elliot bought," she said, tapping the first ad. The page showed a stadium full of cheering people, all wearing Aero Swifts, above the words "Join the millions who already switched." Simon read it twice. Millions. He felt a small pull in his chest, like everyone had a ticket to somewhere and he was still standing outside.

"That doesn't say anything about the shoes," he said slowly. "It just says everyone has them." He flipped to the second magazine. That ad called a rival brand "flimsy" and "a betrayal of your feet," words that made him wince even though he knew nothing about either shoe. The third ad showed a famous sprinter he recognized from television, holding up the shoes and grinning. Milena leaned in. "If he wears them, they must be good." Simon wasn't so sure. The sprinter was being paid, which made the grin feel like camouflage, a smile painted over a sales pitch.

Elliot arrived with a bag of chips and peered at the pages. "My ad worked on me," he admitted. "It said everyone switched, so I switched." Simon straightened up. "That's the trick, though. It wants you to buy them because everyone else did, so you feel like you belong. It never gives you a real reason." He copied the phrase "join the millions" into his notebook, then wrote beside it, what do they actually do better? Underneath, after staring at all three ads, he wrote nothing, because none of them had answered that either.

He tested his idea that evening. Instead of arguing, he showed his mother the ads and pointed out each trick: the crowd, the loaded words, the paid grin of a runner who might be credible about sprinting but had never fixed a sole in his life. "So I don't want them because of the ads," he finished. "I want them because I run every day, and my current pair is coming apart at the heel." His mother studied the ads, then the shoes, then him. She agreed to split the cost, which meant four weekends of raking Mr. Halloran's leaves.

Simon raked all Saturday morning while other kids played soccer in the park across the street, and his blisters throbbed by noon. But when he slid his foot into the new shoes at the store on Sunday, he looked down at them and thought they had come to symbolize something different than belonging. "Notice they're not magic," Milena said, watching him test them in the aisle. "They're just shoes." Simon jogged a slow circle around the racks anyway, grinning, and said, "Yeah, but they're my shoes."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place.
story:
Emilia spread the photocopy of the settler's diary on the cold stone bench beside the war memorial, weighting its corners with two pebbles so the wind wouldn't steal it. Demi sat cross-legged on the grass reading over her shoulder, while Vicky paced the gravel path, reading the names carved into the granite out loud in a low voice, the way people did there. The assignment was due Monday: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, and Emilia had picked a diary written by a Missouri farm family in 1846. So far she had three pages of quotes and no idea how to organize them.

"Here's one," Demi said, tapping a smudged line. "'The bank took the last of the cattle, and Father says the soil is worn out.'" Emilia copied it down. A few entries later they found another: "'Land in Oregon is free to any man who will work it, and the grass grows tall as a horse's belly.' " Vicky wandered back and read both quotes upside down. "So they left because things were bad," she said, "and because Oregon sounded good. Two different kinds of reasons."

Emilia stared at her notebook. The pattern was there, she could feel it, like a shape under a blanket. She wrote "push" beside the first quote and "pull" beside the second. "Something pushed them out of Missouri," she said slowly, "and something pulled them west." She tested it against a third entry, the one where the mother wrote that she'd stay with her sister if not for the letters from a cousin in Oregon describing rivers full of salmon. The cousin was a pull. The worn-out soil and the debt were pushes. Every line in the diary sorted itself onto one side or the other, and Emilia realized this wasn't just her idea for one essay; it was a tool historians actually used, sorting reasons into push factors that drive people away from home and pull factors that attract them to a new place.

"Wait," Demi said. "What about this one? 'The rain persisted all of April and the corn rotted in the ground.' Which side is weather?" Emilia thought. Bad weather made the farm fail, so it pushed them. She wrote it down, feeling the system hold. Then she laughed at herself. Yesterday she'd wanted to quit and copy facts off a website; now she was arguing with Demi about rain.

Ms. Guo, the neighbor who walked her dog past the memorial every afternoon, paused by the bench and glanced at the diary page without saying anything, the way she always did, letting them work. Bees worked the nectar in the flowerbed by the flagpole, moving from bloom to bloom. Vicky, being spontaneous, wrote "PUSH" in block letters on one of Emilia's pebbles and "PULL" on the other, and set them on opposite ends of the bench. "There," she said. "Your outline."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
At 10:43 on a Tuesday night, Tristan's phone buzzed against his desk. The group chat, the one with Caden and Lyam, had gone quiet for two days after the science test, and now it woke up all at once. Lyam had sent eleven messages in a row, none of them spelled correctly, and the last one read: "i cant sleep again. third night. my brain wont shut off."

Tristan sat back down. He had been about to put the phone in the drawer where it lived overnight, because his mom had made that rule back in September and he had actually stuck to it. He read the messages twice. Lyam was usually the loud one, the one who sent videos of himself missing easy shots in gym. This didn't sound like him. It sounded like the words were being typed by someone smaller.

Caden replied first. "same tbh. i just replay the whole day in my head and it's like a virus, one bad thought spreads to all the others." Tristan knew what he meant. He had watched a single missed assignment spread through his whole evening once, ruining dinner and a movie he'd been looking forward to.

He typed, deleted, and typed again. "what do you guys actually do after a bad day." Caden answered fast: "scroll until like 1am." Lyam sent a shrug emoji. Tristan looked at his own answer before sending it. "i shoot hoops at the rec till my legs hurt. then i actually sleep." He paused, then added, "mr greco called that stuff coping. coping means the ways you handle stress or hard feelings. he said the healthy stuff is exercise, enough sleep, or talking to someone you trust."

There was a long pause, the kind you could feel even through a screen. Then Lyam wrote, "wait. talking to someone counts?" "apparently," Tristan sent. "that's literally what we're doing right now." Caden sent three thinking faces, then: "so the 1am scrolling is probably the opposite of that."

Tristan got up, took his basketball from the corner, and balanced it on his palm while he typed one more message. "rec center tomorrow 4pm. lyam you're on my team. caden you're guarding him." He put the phone in the drawer before the replies came, and in the morning he found seventeen new messages, a scouting report from Caden on Lyam's left-handed layup, and a photo of Lyam's sleep app showing six hours and forty minutes.

At 3:52 the next afternoon, Tristan was already at the rec center doors, spinning the ball on one finger, when he saw Lyam walking up the path with his hoodie hood down for the first time all week.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors, because an odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one.
story:
Carson leaned closer to the library computer screen, where his Python program sat half finished in the editor window. He had been working on it for three days now, ever since Karam had bet him a slice of pizza that he could not write code that decided whether a number was prime. The first version had been easy: ask for a number, then test every divisor from 2 upward. It worked. Then Karam typed in 7919, and the program took so long that a spinner appeared in the tab and Carson actually thought the machine had frozen.

"Try it again," Karam said, sliding into the chair beside him. They had claimed the corner spot by the window, the only place in the library with two computers close enough for whispering. "Same number. Maybe it was the internet."

"It's not the internet," Carson whispered. "It's my program. It's testing every single number up to 7919, even ones that can't possibly work." He stared at the loop, counting in his head. That was thousands of pointless checks, all to find out something about one number.

He started trimming the work. First he checked divisibility by 2, and if that failed, he could skip every even divisor after that, because an odd number could never be divided evenly by an even one. He devised a new loop that jumped by twos, hitting only the odd candidates: 3, 5, 7, and on up. Half the work, gone. He ran it again, and 7919 came back labeled prime before the spinner could even appear.

He thought about last summer, when he had quit the swim team after only two weeks because the times on the board stopped improving. His times had hit a plateau and he had walked away, telling himself the pool was the problem. Now he wondered. This program had also seemed stuck, and the answer had not been quitting but looking harder at what was going on underneath.

Karam typed in a long odd number, something with seven digits, and they watched the screen together. The result appeared in under a second, consistent every time they reran it, never once hesitating. "That's not luck," Carson said quietly. "That's half as much work, every single run."

Mr. Thompson, the librarian, appeared behind them with a cart of returns. "Whatever you two are doing over here, keep it down." Then he glanced at the screen and raised an eyebrow. "Is that code?"

"It decides if a number is prime," Carson said. "I made it fast. Want to see?" He cleared the input box and held his hand over the keyboard, grinning at Karam. "Pick the biggest number you know."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Eyeglass prescriptions measure lens strength in diopters, with a minus sign for nearsightedness and a plus sign for farsightedness.
story:
Sawyer sat very still in the big chair at the optometrist's office, holding a slip of paper with numbers printed on it. One line read OD -2.00, and the more he stared at it, the worse he felt. He had squinted through the whole eye exam, guessed at letters, and now it seemed his eyes had scored negative two. Out of what, he wondered. A hundred? Zero?

His mother was still at the front desk sorting out the insurance, so Sawyer turned to the girl in the next chair, who was waiting for her own appointment. "Do you know what this means?" he asked, hesitant to sound like a total stranger quizzing her, but he showed her the slip anyway. "I think my eyes got a minus score."

The girl, whose name tag on her backpack said Phoenix, leaned over and looked. "That's the lens strength," she said. "Diopters. The minus sign means nearsighted." She held up her own paper, which read +1.50. "Plus means farsighted. I'm the opposite of you."

Sawyer turned both slips around in his mind. Minus for nearsighted, plus for farsighted, and the number was how strong the lens was, not a grade. So his eyes hadn't failed a test. His lenses just needed a certain strength to fix a certain problem. He decided to test the idea before he believed it. "So if somebody had zero, they'd need no glasses at all?"

"Zero would mean no lens," Phoenix said, grinning. "You'd have an empty frame. Fashion glasses."

A woman in a white coat came out then and called his name, and while she fitted the new frames over his ears, Sawyer noticed a tray of lenses on the counter, each one in a labeled slot. Minus numbers on one side, plus numbers on the other, getting bigger as they went. It matched what Phoenix had said, and he felt something settle in his chest, like a math problem snapping into place.

He walked to the front where his mother stood with the cashier, and through the new lenses the room jumped out at him, sharp and surprising. The clock on the far wall had hands. The poster by the door had actual words on it instead of gray smudges. On the bus ride home he texted his friend Tatum, "guess what, minus two isn't bad, it's just nearsighted. Phoenix explained it." Then he looked out the window and read the sign across the street out loud, just because he could.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, wherefore means why, so Juliet's line "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" asks why he has to be Romeo, not where he is.
story:
Payton sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with the balcony scene spread out in front of her and a pencil behind her ear. Ms. Kapoor had assigned each pair of students one speech from Romeo and Juliet to paraphrase into modern English, and Payton had drawn Juliet's most famous line. Tomorrow she and Rowan would stand up in class and read the original, then read their version. Payton's draft already covered three lines, and she was proud of the third one, which she thought sounded smooth.

Rowan arrived at four with a plastic bag of crackers and the confidence of someone who had not yet started. "So you did the whole thing?" Rowan said, flopping onto the bed. "Show me."

Payton handed over her notebook. Rowan read in a slow mumble, then stopped and frowned. "Wait. This part. Juliet says, 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' and you wrote that she's asking where he is. Like she's looking around for him."

"She's on a balcony," Payton said. "He's hiding in the garden. She's trying to find him. That makes sense."

"Does it, though?" Rowan popped a cracker in her mouth and chewed, staring at the page. "If she wanted to know where he was, she'd say 'where art thou.' Not 'wherefore.'"

Payton took the notebook back and looked at the line again. She had assumed the word meant what it sounded like, but Rowan was right that the extra syllable had to be there for a reason. She flipped to the glossary at the back of the paperback and ran her finger down the W's. Wherefore: why. She read it twice. Then she read Juliet's line out loud, slowly, and something clicked into place like the last piece of a puzzle she hadn't known she was solving.

"She's not asking where he is," Payton said. "She's asking why he has to be Romeo. Why does he have to be a Montague, her family's enemy. That's the whole point of the scene. She just fell for the one person she's supposed to oppose."

Rowan sat up. "So she's arguing with fate. Not hiding from her nurse."

"Exactly." Payton crossed out her smooth-sounding sentence and started over. "It's like Gloria complaining about the cafeteria prices. She doesn't want to know where her money goes. She wants to know why the school needs all that revenue from seventh graders buying cardboard pizza."

Rowan laughed. "That is actually a perfect paraphrase. Can we use that?"

"Gloria would love it." Payton wrote the new version out, then tested it the way she'd test a math answer, by plugging it back in. If wherefore meant why, then the rest of the speech lined up: Juliet goes straight from that line to "What's in a name?" She's questioning the whole idea that names matter. If wherefore meant where, the next lines would make no sense at all. Every line fit the new reading. She underlined it.

"Last week I turned in a vocab sheet without checking anything," Rowan said quietly, snapping a cracker in half. "Guessed on half of it. Got a C minus." She looked at the crossed-out sentence in Payton's notebook. "I kind of wish I'd done what you just did. Look it up before I decided I knew."

Payton didn't answer right away, because she'd been about to walk into class tomorrow with the wrong meaning, sure of herself. She wondered how many times she'd done that already without ever finding out. "Then we check everything," she said finally. "Every weird word, tonight. Even if it takes until dinner."

Rowan dragged the book closer and pointed at a line near the bottom of the page. "Start with 'doth.'"

Payton flipped to the glossary, already running her finger down the page.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: A thicker wire of the same material and length has less resistance than a thinner one, because current has more room to flow.
story:
Raphael spread his kit on the picnic table by the playground fence: a battery pack, a multimeter, and two coils of copper wire, one fat, one skinny. The science fair was in nine days, and his project was a mess. He knew the formula, voltage divided by current equals resistance, but every time he measured, the numbers came out strange.

"Still out here?" Lexy asked, dropping onto the opposite bench. She peeled an orange while a squirrel, some fat gray rodent, watched her from the top of the fence.

"Watch this," Raphael said. He clipped the thick wire to the battery, touched the meter probes to each end, and wrote down the voltage. Then he broke the circuit and clipped the meter in to read the current. He divided. "Point eight ohms. Fine. That's approximate, but fine."

"That's the number you wanted?"

"Sort of. Now the weird part." He swapped in the thin wire, the same copper, cut to the same length. He measured again, tongue between his teeth, and the answer came out more than three times bigger. "Two point nine ohms. Same battery, same length. It makes no sense. The wire isn't broken. I checked."

Lexy leaned over the notebook. Outside the fence, kids were yelling across the monkey bars, and dew had begun to condense on the slide, so it shone in the streetlight like it was made of glass. "Maybe the meter's wrong," she said.

"That's what I thought." Raphael had a second idea, though, one he could actually test. He found the fat wire's cut end and the thin wire's cut end, laid them side by side on the table, and stared at them. One was as round as a pencil, the other barely thicker than thread. "Same copper. Same length. The only thing different is how thick it is."

"So?"

"So let me see if thickness is doing it." He doubled the thin wire back on itself, twisted the two strands together, and clipped the doubled wire into the circuit. If thickness mattered, two strands side by side should act like one thicker wire. He measured the voltage, measured the current, divided. "One point four. It dropped. Not all the way down to point eight, but way down from two point nine."

Lexy sat up straight, orange forgotten. "Wait. So the thick one has less resistance than the thin one?"

"Same stuff, same length, yeah." Raphael said it slowly, testing the idea as he spoke. "A thicker wire of the same material and length has less resistance than a thinner one." He underlined his numbers twice. "That's why my readings were freaking out. I kept assuming all copper was the same."

Braden jogged over from the basketball court, sweating, and looked at the pile of clips and wire. "You're doing homework at the playground?"

"Better," Raphael said. "I found a rule." He pulled out a fresh page and wrote a new title across the top: Why Wire Thickness Matters. "I'm going to test three more thicknesses tomorrow. Want to hold the probes?"

Braden wiped his hands on his shorts and picked up the meter. "Red goes where again?"

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: Two things happening together, a correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; a third factor may cause both.
story:
Olivia flipped her notebook to a fresh page and wrote CLAIM, EVIDENCE, WARRANT across the top in block letters. The mini-tournament started at four o'clock, and Ms. Aquino had been clear: every point had to have all three, or the judges would tear it apart. She and Jase had drawn the side arguing that the town should keep its outdoor summer pool open later, and so far all they had was a stack of articles and three hours.

Jase slid into the chair across from her with a granola bar and a triumphant grin. "Found it. The perfect evidence. Pool attendance goes up in June, and so do ice cream sales at the shop next door. So keeping the pool open later boosts local business. Claim, evidence, done."

Olivia frowned at his printout. Something about it bothered her, a pattern she couldn't quite see yet. "But wait. Ice cream sales go up in July too, and sunburns go up in July. Would you say ice cream causes sunburn?"

Jase laughed. "Obviously not."

"Right. So two things rising together doesn't prove one caused the other." She tapped her pencil, testing the idea. "Maybe a third thing causes both. Like the sun. Heat makes people buy ice cream and makes people swim and makes people burn." She wrote THIRD FACTOR in her notebook and underlined it twice. "So for our pool argument, we can't just say attendance and ice cream rise together. We need to show the pool itself brings people who wouldn't come otherwise."

Jase looked at his printout, then at her notebook, then shut his laptop. "Okay. Okay, I'm convinced. Let's rebuild the case."

They spent the next hour hunting for evidence that actually linked the pool to the town, not just to summer. Jude wandered over from the prep table and tried to evade their questions about his side, but when Olivia showed him the ice cream example, he stopped, reread it, and changed his mind about his own strongest point. "My hospital stats have the same problem," he muttered. "I'm cutting them."

By four, the rec hall had gone almost tranquil, the way it did right before a round began. Olivia stood at the podium, laid out her claim about the pool, cited the survey of families who said they came to the pool and stayed for dinner afterward, and gave her warrant: the pool, not the season, was the reason they came. She won on a two-to-one decision.

Afterward, Jase bought her a celebratory ice cream from the camp store, and they sat on the steps in the late sun. Olivia took one bite and winced at the sting on her shoulders.

"Sunburn's worse," Jase observed. "And you ate the most ice cream. Very suspicious."

"Blame the third factor," she said, and held out the cone.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Detergent molecules have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water.
story:
The note from her mom, stuck to the fridge that morning, read like a treasure map: "You said you wanted to learn laundry, so here it is. Sort by colour, check pockets, cold water, and do NOT use the whole bottle of detergent like your brother did. Budget it, Alexia. One capful. Love, Mom." Alexia had read it three times, folded it into her pocket, and now she was standing in the detergent aisle of the grocery store with Jameson, both of them staring at a wall of bottles like it was a museum exhibit.

"Okay," she said, grabbing a red bottle. "Here's the thing. My shirt has the pizza grease from Friday on it, and I already tried washing it with just water in the sink. Nothing. It just sat there, like it was living there now, some kind of greasy organism." Jameson laughed so hard a woman with a cart gave them a look. "That's why we need this stuff. My theory is detergent actually does something water can't do."

Mr. Hosseini, their neighbour, turned the corner with his own basket and raised an eyebrow at them. "Doing science in aisle nine?" he asked. "Something like that," Alexia said. He held up his hands like he was refusing to get involved, but he was smiling.

At home, they sorted her laundry into piles on the living room floor, darks, whites, and one lonely pink sock that Alexia held up like evidence. "Whose is this?" Jameson said, "Not mine, I don't even own anything pink," and the way he said it, too fast and too loud, made her squint at him until he cracked and pulled the matching sock out of his own hoodie pocket. "It's Camden's. He said if I stole it he'd counterfeit my signature on the group project sign-up sheet. Don't ask." She laughed and threw both socks into the dark pile, because pink plus red plus wet clearly equalled disaster, and she wasn't taking chances.

She checked every pocket, measured exactly one capful, and started the machine. When it finished, she pulled out the pizza shirt and spread it flat on the dryer. The grease spot was gone. Genuinely gone. "It worked," she whispered, then louder, shoving the shirt at Jameson. "Look! It's gone! The detergent grabbed it!" She told him her theory: the detergent had to be lifting the grease off the fabric and carrying it away into the water, because water alone had done nothing at all. "So the stuff isn't just soap water," she said. "It's basically got to have one end that grabs grease and one end that grabs water. That's the only way it works." Jameson leaned in close to the fabric, hunting for the ghost of the stain. "You should text your mom a picture." She did, then folded the warm shirt into a neat square, her very first one, and set it on top of the dryer like a trophy.
